text: Without RBAC, every new hire means someone manually figuring out what permissions they need and running one-off grants against their personal login. Role-based access control breaks that into two separate questions: what does a role need, and who belongs to it.

SQL Server implements this directly with database roles. You create a role, then grant permissions to the role, never to an individual user. Three GRANT statements aimed at a SalesAnalystRole define its entire entitlement, and every person later added to that role inherits all three immediately, no need to re-touch a hundred individual logins.

ALTER ROLE ADD MEMBER puts a user into a role, that's a Joiner or Mover event from last lesson becoming a one-line operation. ALTER ROLE DROP MEMBER removes them, that's a Mover or Leaver event. A Joiner gets added to the right role, a Mover gets dropped from the old one and added to the new, a Leaver gets dropped from every role they were in.

Three permission statements look similar but behave differently. GRANT gives a permission. REVOKE removes a previously granted one, back to a neutral state. DENY explicitly blocks a permission, and DENY always wins, even if the user also belongs to a different role that grants the same permission. You can DENY down to a single column, blocking just the SSN column while the role still grants SELECT on the rest of the table.

The payoff isn't fewer keystrokes, it's answerability. An auditor can answer who can see customer SSNs by reading a handful of role permissions instead of auditing every login. Next up: least privilege, the rule that decides what a role's permissions should actually be.
